title: The Robots are Here: Navigating the Generative AI Revolution in Computing Education
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education V. 2 (ITiCSE 2023)
extended_summary:
This working group report examines how large language models (LLMs) and generative AI are reshaping computing education. The paper addresses several related questions: what the existing research says about LLMs in computing education, how students and instructors currently perceive these tools, how educators are already adapting pedagogy and assessment, what ethical issues arise, and how well current models perform on computing education tasks. The goal is to provide a broad evidence-based overview of opportunities, risks, and emerging practices as generative AI becomes widely available in educational settings.

The paper uses multiple approaches rather than testing a single intervention. It includes a scoping review of 71 primary articles on LLMs in computing education, an international survey of computing students and instructors from 20 countries, in-depth interviews with 22 computing educators across five continents, an ethics analysis framed by the ACM Code of Ethics and university AI policies, and benchmarking/replication work evaluating LLM performance on computing education datasets. Across these components, the paper focuses on the use of tools such as ChatGPT, GPT models, Codex, and GitHub Copilot in programming and computer science teaching and assessment.

The populations and contexts span computing students, computing instructors, and educators working in higher education and related professional academic settings across multiple countries. The report is not limited to one classroom or institution; instead, it synthesizes literature and collects international perspectives from participants in diverse regions. The educational context is primarily computing education, especially introductory and higher education programming courses, with attention to pedagogy, assessment, academic integrity, and learner support.

The paper concludes that generative AI is already having a substantial impact on computing education and will continue to do so. It identifies major opportunities, such as personalized support, code explanations, reduced instructor workload, and new forms of assessment and learning activities, while also highlighting serious risks including over-reliance, inaccurate outputs, academic integrity challenges, bias, and inequitable benefits. The authors argue that educators and institutions should adapt thoughtfully rather than simply prohibit these tools, and they position the report as a focal resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to evaluate and integrate LLM-based tools in computing classrooms.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Large language models and generative AI tools used in computing education, including code generation, explanation, feedback, and teaching-material creation systems.
identified_tools.use_case: This working group report reviews 71 primary articles on LLMs/generative AI in computing education, surveys students and instructors, interviews educators, discusses ethics/policy, and benchmarks model performance across computing education datasets. It does not provide a per-tool causal evaluation of a single named product.

findings.finding_summary: Across 71 primary articles in computing education, LLMs were generally reported to perform at a level equivalent to or better than average students on code-generation tasks, but less well on other tasks such as multiple-choice questions, Parsons problems, and computational thinking tasks. The paper reports no pooled meta-analytic effect size or confidence interval.
findings.measure: Literature synthesis of LLM performance on computing education tasks (e.g., code generation, MCQs, Parsons problems, computational thinking tasks)

findings.finding_summary: The review synthesis reports that LLMs can provide better code explanations than students and can explain answers to textbook questions in about half of cases. The paper does not report pooled effect sizes or confidence intervals for these outcomes.
findings.measure: Quality/usefulness of code explanations and textbook-answer explanations in reviewed studies

findings.finding_summary: Reviewed studies suggest LLMs can reduce instructor workload by generating teaching materials, supporting grading-related tasks, and providing personalized help to struggling students. The paper presents this as a synthesis of prior work rather than a quantified pooled estimate.
findings.measure: Instructor workload reduction and automation of educational support tasks

findings.finding_summary: The report synthesizes evidence that AI code generators can improve novice programming productivity in some studies, citing one study where students using AI code generators performed significantly better with 1.15x progress, 0.59x errors, 1.8x higher correctness, and 0.57x time spent, but also notes risks of over-reliance, confusion, and unequal benefits favoring more knowledgeable students. No pooled effect size is reported.
findings.measure: Programming productivity, correctness, errors, time spent, and learning risks in human-AI programming contexts
findings.effect_size: 1.15x progress; 0.59x errors; 1.8x higher correctness; 0.57x time spent (as cited from one reviewed study)

findings.finding_summary: The paper concludes that generative AI poses substantial assessment and academic-integrity challenges because LLMs perform very well on common introductory programming assessments, while also creating opportunities to rethink assessment toward problem solving, code understanding, tracing, verification, and code review. These are synthesis conclusions rather than pooled quantitative estimates.
findings.measure: Implications for assessment design, academic integrity, and curriculum adaptation in computing education

quality_tier_rationale: This is a scoping/working-group review with survey and interview components, not a meta-analysis or single causal impact study. It synthesizes a broad evidence base, but findings are largely narrative and heterogeneous rather than pooled quantitatively.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial promise and substantial risks, with mixed directions across outcomes and no pooled effect sizes. Overall impact is important but quantitatively unclear at the aggregate level.
